Note from the hostel office, Tuesday.
Noor knocked on my door on the twenty-third and asked to borrow enough for a bus pass. She said she had "bought nothing big this month" and looked honestly puzzled. I did not lend it straight away. Instead we sat at my table and she opened her payment history. Step one, we wrote down every spend over the month. Step two, we circled the repeats. There were nineteen late-night food orders, a music plan, a video plan and a study-notes subscription she had forgotten. No single item was large. Together they came to more than her mess fees. Noor went quiet, then laughed a little and said, "It was the samosas at midnight." Step three, she cancelled two subscriptions while sitting there. I lent the bus fare and we agreed she would come back on the first to plan the next month.
Nikita, hostel warden

qa.a: Noor knocked on the door on the twenty-third.

qa.q: How did Noor feel when the circled repeats were added up?
qa.a: Noor felt embarrassed and a bit stunned: she went quiet, then laughed a little and admitted it was the midnight samosas.

qa.a: Writing down every spend and circling the repeats helped most, because it showed that many small orders, not one big buy, had emptied the month.

qa.q: What would change if Nikita had simply lent the money at the door?
qa.a: Noor would have got through the week but still not known where the money went, so the same gap could open again next month.

grounding: Illustrates a student who runs short before month end and discovers that small repeated food orders and forgotten subscriptions added up.

26th, night.
Balance: almost nothing, and payday is five days away. Afreen saw my face at dinner and said, "Trisha, you keep checking that app like it will change." It won't. I have not bought a single big thing since my first salary came. No phone, no shoes, nothing. So where did it go?
I finally scrolled through the whole month. Chai and a sandwich delivered to the office every afternoon, because the canteen line is long. Three streaming plans, one of them from a free trial I never cancelled. Two cab rides a week when I was "too tired" for the metro. Each one felt like nothing.
I wrote them all in the back of this diary and added them up twice. Tomorrow I will cancel two plans and ask Afreen if we can cook on weekdays. Feeling foolish, but also a bit less lost.

qa.a: Chai and a sandwich were delivered to the office every afternoon.

The electronics shop near the Barabanki bus stand had a banner: ZERO DOWN PAYMENT. Afreen stopped. Her old laptop had died in the middle of her second-year project.
Abhinav, the young salesman, smiled. "Just sign here, didi. Small amount every month, that's all." He added a mixer-grinder for her mother at the same "easy" rate. Afreen went home feeling proud; Ammi hugged her over the new mixer.

In Lisbon, the self-checkout beeped: card declined. Omar stared at the basket of rice, eggs and coffee. Behind him, Yosef raised an eyebrow.
"I had money yesterday," Omar muttered.
On the tram home he opened his banking app. Three pay-later instalments had come out that morning: the gaming chair, the concert tickets, the winter jacket. Each one had looked tiny at checkout, a quarter of the price, split so neatly. He had never lined them up on the same calendar.
Yosef bought the groceries and didn't make a joke of it. At the kitchen table that night, Omar listed every plan, every date and every late fee he had already paid. The total made his face go hot. "No more splitting," he said. "Not till these are done." He deleted the pay-later option from his saved cards and set the dates in his calendar.

I stopped opening the bank envelopes. I sleep badly. Last week you asked why I skipped your birthday dinner, and I said work. It was not work. I could not face paying for anyone's meal.
I am telling you first because you won't panic. I have made a list of every card, loan and due date. On Saturday I want to go to the bank and ask about a repayment plan, and I want you to come. After that, we tell Amma together.
Your brother,
Pankaj

Hemant, you've known me since school, and you know Uday was always the one who paid for chai. That was part of the problem. Last year I had two cards and a personal loan, and I was using each one to pay the next. My wife thought the bonus had cleared everything. I let her think that.
Every time my phone buzzed I thought it was the bank. I stopped answering unknown numbers. I snapped at my son over homework. It wasn't homework I was angry at.
What changed? One night I just said it at dinner. My wife was quiet for a long time, then she said, "Why didn't you tell me when it was small?" We went to the bank together and they set up a plan with fixed dates. A counsellor there explained which loan to close first. It's still not done. But I sleep now, yaar. I wish I had spoken a year earlier.

April. He woke at 3 a.m. two nights running, adding numbers in his head. At work he typed the wrong figure in an invoice. When Rehana asked if he was all right, he said, "Tired, that's all." That Sunday she found the statement fallen behind the sofa.
May. They sat at the dining table with a notebook. Jomon wrote every card, every balance and every date. Rehana did not lecture; she just asked, "Which bank do we call first?" On Monday he met a debt counsellor at his bank. By the end of May he had closed the third card and was paying on one plan with one date.

Papa called again after lunch. Naveen's wedding hall needs an advance, and the caterer too, and "you are the one with the city job, beta." I said yes before he finished. Of course I said yes. Naveen is my little brother and I love him.

When my scooter's engine seized last winter, I was more annoyed than scared. That surprised me. Two years earlier, a repair like that would have gone on a card and followed me for months.
What changed was dull, honestly. After my first job, a senior at work, Madhav, showed me his spreadsheet. He paid every bill on the same few dates. Savings moved out the day salary landed. On the last Sunday of each month, he spent twenty minutes looking at where it had gone. I copied all of it, a bit grudgingly.
The first few months felt tight. Then I stopped thinking about it. The reserve grew slowly, and I nearly forgot it was there until the mechanic handed me the bill. I paid it and went home.
I'm Arnab, and I used to think discipline meant willpower. Mostly it meant setting things up once so I didn't need any.

qa.a: The scooter's engine seized last winter.

My name is Pallavi, and last year I went to the municipal office three times for one birth certificate correction.
The first time, I reached at noon. The guard pointed me to counter four. Counter four sent me to counter seven. Counter seven said, "Bring a photocopy of your mother's ID," and shut the window for lunch. I stood in the corridor feeling stupid and close to tears.
The second time I had the photocopy, but not the original. A different clerk wanted both.
Before the third trip, I called my neighbour Seema aunty, who had done the same correction for her son. She dictated a list: originals, two photocopies of each, passport photos, the affidavit. She told me to reach before the doors opened. I did. I was fourth in line, and I was out by eleven.

Every morning Gurpreet drove the school van through the lanes of Nabha, picking up eleven children before eight. He knew every pothole and which child always ran late.
On a Tuesday in July, a traffic constable waved the van over near the grain market. "Licence." Gurpreet handed it over with a smile. The constable turned it. "Expired in April."

He called Ganga, who ran the school's transport, and she sent another driver while Gurpreet waited by the road with the children. The school kept him off the van until he had renewed.
That evening his daughter wrote every renewal date on the kitchen calendar in big red letters and set phone reminders for all of them. Gurpreet went to the transport office on Thursday morning.

In Toronto, the envelope was thin and official. Noa opened it standing in the hallway and read it twice. Late filing: a penalty and interest on last year's tax return.
She had meant to do it in April. Then work got busy, and the receipts sat in a shoebox under the bed. Nobody had reminded her. Nobody ever does, she thought.
At lunch she told her colleague Siddiq. He pulled out his phone and showed her his calendar: tax deadline, car registration, health card renewal, each with a reminder two weeks ahead and another two days ahead.
"It's boring," he said. "That's the point. I don't have to remember anything."
That night Noa emptied the shoebox onto the table, filed the return, and paid the penalty. Then she opened her calendar and entered every renewal she could find in her drawer. Five of them. One was due next month.

Anjali, sit. Your Damini maasi will tell you about my first pension claim, the year after your nana retired.
I was twenty-five. The clerk at the district office kept my file under a stack of others for six weeks. Each time I went, he said, "Some paper is missing." Never which paper. Once he rubbed his thumb and finger together and smiled. I went home and cried in the bathroom, so angry I could not eat.
My friend Beena said, "Don't shout, and don't pay. Ask him to write down the rule." So next time I stood at his window and said, very politely, "Sir, kindly write which paper is missing and under which order." He stopped smiling. Then I asked where the grievance box was. The file moved in four days.
I was shaking the whole time, Anjali. Polite is not the same as weak.

Your brother,
